name: Gende
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 12 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Capell, Arthur. 1948. Distribution of languages in the Central Highlands, New Guinea [Part I: Phonetics]. Oceania 19(2): 104-129. Group-level statement covering all Central Highlands languages of the 1947 survey; Gende listed under the Chimbu Group (p. 106). Gende-specific accent data in Part II (Oceania 19(3): 234-253, pp. 236 and 245) and Part III (Oceania 19(4): 349-377, Chimbu vocabulary pp. 363-366).
catalog_locator: Oceania 19(2), p. 110, last paragraph of Part I before 'PART II. GRAMMAR'. Saved scan. Scope sentences: p. 106 table (Gende = Chimbu Group C), p. 107 'Part I rests entirely on personal observation by the writer'. Gende data: Part II p. 236 (possessives, crop); Part II p. 245 (dubitative -vá 'with accent', crop); Part III pp. 363-366 (Gende column crops, pp365-366).
catalog_quote: Accent is rather variable; where it does not fall on the antepenultimate, it is marked in the vocabularies and sentences. Some of the languages have a musical intonation; none, however, employs tone with a semantic significance. The above outline of the phonetic system of the Central Highlands languages will serve the purposes of the present paper.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check:, PDF page 20 = Oceania 19(2) p. 110 (running head 'DISTRIBUTION OF LANGUAGES', last paragraph before 'PART II. GRAMMAR'). extracted text gives exactly: 'Accent is rather variable; where it does not fall on the antepenultimate, it is marked in the vocabularies and sentences. Some of the languages have a musical intonation; none, however, employs tone with a semantic significance. The above outline of the phonetic system of the Central Highlands languages will serve the purposes of the present paper.' Also at line 1512 of. Verbatim, including the spaced semicolons. Context read: Part I (pp. 104-110) is Capell's own field phonetics from a 1947 survey; p. 107 states 'Part I rests e…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Central Highlands languages as a group (Gende included), accent falls by default on the antepenultimate syllable; it is 'rather variable', and words whose accent is elsewhere are individually marked; no lexical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Accent is rather variable'; wherever it is not antepenultimate Capell marks it in the word lists (no rule given for the deviations). No language of the survey uses tone semantically.
new_statements.domain_note: Blanket characterisation of the phonetic system of ALL Central Highlands languages in Capell's survey (Gende is listed in his Chimbu Group, p. 106, and he states that vocabularies were worked out only for Kuman and Gende), not a Gende-specific statement; word level (vocabulary citation forms and sentences). Burgmann 1953: 264, relaying Aufenanger, says Capell's Gende material needs checking and lists several errors in his Gende forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell's 'Gende' (Chimbu Group, Bundi area, Oceania 1948-49) and Aufenanger's Gende (Bundi-Nombri dialect spoken at the Bundi mission station) are the same language as gend1249; no separate dialect glottocode exists. The quoted accent statement is a group-level generalisation over all Central Highlands languages in Capell's survey, not a description of Gende alone.

sources.locator: printed p. 170, section 10.2.2; cf. footnote 32, printed p. 22
sources.note: No Gende-specific statement on stress, accent or tone anywhere in the chapter or book. The only prosodic statement is the family-level sentence quoted (tone OR stress, unresolved per language). Footnote 32 (printed p. 22) lists East-Central languages recorded as tonal (Siane, Gahuku, Gimi) and as stress-based (Benabena, Kamano, Yagaria); Gende is not named in either list. Gende appendix wordlist forms (Gn) carry no stress or tone marks; Gende data follow Aufenanger 1952 (footnote 180, printed p. 174) and Z'graggen 1971 'Gende Wordlist' (in preparation). Nothing here bears on the catalog's Cape

sources.note: Gende = K1 (East New Guinea Highlands Stock), 6,143 speakers, village list (Bundi, Yandera etc.); bibliography lists Aufenanger 1938, 1952, 1960 and Aufenanger & Höltker 1940. No phonology.

sources.citation: Wurm, S. A. 1964. Phonological diversification in Australian New Guinea Highlands languages. Pacific Linguistics B-2. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Gives Gende (2a, East-Central family) consonant and vowel inventories and computes phonological-diversification indices; concludes Gende is 'a phonologically aberrant language'. Stress/accent is not among the features treated; no mention for Gende.

sources.citation: Burgmann, Arnold. 1953. H. Aufenangers Vokabular und Grammatik der Gende-Sprache in Zentral-Neuguinea (Micro-Bibliotheca Anthropos, Vol. 1). Anthropos 48: 263-267.
sources.note: Extended review of the 1952 microfilm grammar: Bundi-Nombri dialect, 96-page vocabulary (~3500 words), grammar as 'Rohmaterial' with a 'Lautlehre (185-188)' section, texts. Gives the table of contents only; silent on stress. Also notes Capell's Gende data 'bedarf.. der Überprüfung' (p. 264, with corrections from Aufenanger).

sources.note: Chimbu-group grammar notes; Gende pronouns, possessives, verb 'requires separate treatment'; 'full investigation has been carried out only in Kuman and Gende'. No stress statement for Gende (only a Kuman suffix '-vá (with accent)').

sources.citation: Aufenanger, Heinrich. 1938. Etwas über Zahl und Zählen bei den Gende im Bismarckgebirge Neuguineas. Anthropos 33: 273-277.
sources.note: Numerals in the Bundi-Nombri dialect carry acute accent marks in the scanned (mápro 'one', oró-gu-mago 'three', karamá, ogonderóri, gineisá), i.e. accent placement varies across words, but there is no statement of a stress rule.
